source.title: The survival double descent: generalization dynamics of deep neural networks in time-to-event analysis

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, though some equations and symbols are garbled by text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests model-capacity double descent in a new setting: synthetic survival data and Cox neural networks, using concordance and integrated Brier score.
record.gate_note: The study sweeps network width and reports test concordance and IBS. It does not sweep training epochs or training sample size; all models train for 10,000 epochs and the data split is fixed. The interpolation threshold location is reported, but no results compare alternative measures of effective complexity across size, epoch, and sample axes. High-censoring results vary censoring, not sample count.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps the width of two-hidden-layer DeepSurv networks on synthetic survival data and reports held-out concordance and IBS. That is a model-wise double-descent test in a new setting (Cox partial likelihood, censored outcomes). It also compares one weight-decay value against no regularization.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that width-wise double descent occurs in concordance for neural Cox models, though the recovered value does not significantly exceed width 2 (p = 0.07). IBS saturates at about 0.52 regardless of capacity or regularization. They call this calibration failure their central finding and attribute it to extreme risk scores breaking the Breslow estimator. High censoring obscures the pattern, and weight decay gives a non-significant gain in worst-case concordance without fixing calibration.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a width sweep of deep networks and held-out performance, but studies synthetic time-to-event data trained with Cox partial likelihood and measures concordance and IBS rather than the original settings’ general test error.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pattern varies by covariate scenario and censoring: categorical inputs show no double descent, high censoring obscures the dip, and nonlinear ground truth retains it. Weight decay 0.01 attenuates the concordance dip but does not improve IBS.

fits_no_version.finding: Calibration (IBS) decouples from discrimination. Neural Cox models produce extreme risk scores (about ±15) that make Breslow survival estimates degenerate at all widths and under weight decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under ranking-based losses, double descent can appear in a ranking metric while calibration error saturates rather than descending again.

record.problems: All results are from synthetic data and a fixed two-hidden-layer architecture. The study uses 20 seeds per condition; it reports that high-censoring variance obscures the pattern and that the regularization comparison is not statistically significant. Width is varied with fixed optimization hyperparameters. The categorical scenario remains near chance, so it cannot establish the curve in that setting.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results left out.

untested.parts: Only fixed depth (two layers), a fixed optimizer and synthetic survival data; no image or text tasks and no depth sweep.
All parts: training is fixed at 10,000 epochs and no curve over epochs is reported.
All parts: the sample size is fixed (600 training samples).
All parts: only neural networks are swept over capacity; Cox PH and RSF are fixed baselines.
All parts: the peak is located only on the width axis. Whether events or n set the threshold is raised, but Scenario D is inconclusive.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes it. Only one weight decay (0.01) was tested.
All parts: no re-expression against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Location of the peak: 625 parameters at width 16, between n = 600 and about 420 events. This was used to ask whether events or n govern the threshold.
missing.locator: Results, Baseline Double Descent Curve; Introduction question 2

missing.what: Full width sweep (2 to 2048) in Figure 1, including recovery beyond width 64. Only widths 2, 16 and 2048 are tabulated.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The Scenario C challenge label was removed because the models fail at chance level. The V1 label for weight decay was removed because regularization bears on V6. The width-16 threshold is fixed by design in Table 3 for all scenarios, so peak location is not independently estimated per scenario.

versions.untested_parts: Tests width-wise behavior in survival models using concordance and IBS, not generic test error across other deep-network settings.
No test-error trajectory over training epochs is reported.
Only neural networks are swept over capacity; Cox PH and random survival forest are fixed comparators, not capacity sweeps across model classes.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
Tests one weight-decay setting (0.01), but not whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
No curve is re-expressed against an effective parameter count to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shape.

rows.measure: Test integrated Brier score (IBS; lower indicates better calibration)
rows.value: Width 16: 0.523 ± 0.035; width 2048: 0.523 ± 0.036; text describes a plateau of approximately 0.523 ± 0.035 for widths ≥ 16.
rows.locator: Results, Baseline Double Descent Curve; Table 2
rows.note: Unlike concordance, IBS rises from the small-width result and then plateaus; the text says calibration does not recover in the overparameterized regime.
rows.check: IBS rises from 0.448 to about 0.523 and stays flat, with no second descent. The authors attribute this to extreme risk scores breaking the Breslow estimator at all capacities, not to the capacity curve itself. State is absent for the second descent.
